source_text: Sed ista, inquit, genera quinque illas naturas inhabitantia saeua erant atque pestifera. quasi ego in eis saeuitiam pestemque laudauerim. ecce, ego tecum uitupero, quae in illis mala esse criminaris, lauda tu mecum, quae in illis bona ipse commemoras: ita uidebis bona malis permixta te uelle constituere pro summo et extremo malo. uitupero ibi tecum pestem, lauda ibi mecum salutem; non enim genera illa uel gigni uel nutriri uel inhabitare illam terram sine aliqua salute potuissent. uitupero ibi tecum tenebras, lauda ibi mecum fecunditatem; tenebras enim dicis „inaestimabiles. et addis tamen "cum propriis fetibus," quamquam tenebrae non sunt corporeae totumque hoc nomen lucis absentia est, sicut nuditas carere uestitu et inanitas uacare corporis plenitudine; ac propterea tenebrae nihil gignere potuerunt, quamuis terra potuerit tenebrosa, id est carens luce aliquid gignere. sed interim hoc omittamus. fetus tamen ubi exoriuntur, et temperamentum est aptum saluti et quaedam concordia numerosa ordinat atque in unitatem coaedificat membra nascentium sibimet inuicem moderationis pace congruentia. quae omnia quis non intellegat maiore laude quam tenebras uituperatione dignanda? uitupero ibi tecum caenum turbidum aquarum, lauda ibi mecum et ipsam speciem qualitatemque aquarum et inhabitatorum natantium membra congruentia, uitam corpus continentem et regentem et omne temperamentum sui generis ualetudini adcommodatum. quantumuis enim aquas caenosas turbidasque reprehendas, eo tamen, quod tales aquas dicis, ut animantia sua possent et gignere et continere, speciem illis qualiscumque corporis et partium similitudinem, qua in unam formantur pacanturque qualitatem, auferre non potes, quia si abstuleris, nullum erit corpus: quae omnia, si es homo, sentis esse laudanda. et quantumuis illorum inhabitatorum saeuitiam et inter se impetus dilacerationis et uastationis exaggeres, non eis tamen adimis numerosos formarum terminos, quibus sibi singula eorum corpora membrorum parilitate pacata sunt, et temperamentum salutis, et moderamen animae partes sui corporis in unitatem amicitiae concordiaeque redigentis: quae si humano sensu intueris, uides plus esse laudanda quam illa uituperanda, quae displicent. uitupero ibi tecum horrorem uentorum, lauda ibi mecum eorundem uentorum spirabilem nutricemque naturam et speciem corporis conuenientia partium continuati atque diffusi : quibus rebus omnibus illos inhabitatores suos poterant et gignere et \' alere et salubriter continere eorumque inhabitatorum, cum cetera, quae in omnibus animantibus superiore ratione laudata sunt, tum proprie inpigros et faciles unde uelint et quo uelint transitus et alarum in uolatu concordem nisum et non inparem motum. uitupero ibi tecum corruptionem ignis, lauda ibi mecum genitabilem ignem et uigentem oportunamque eius temperationem nascentibus, et ut coalescerent et ut suis numeris liniamentisque perficerentur et ut uiuere atque habitare ibi possent: quae omnia non solum in ignis habitatione, sed in ipsis quoque habitantibus miranda et laudanda esse cognoscis. uitupero ibi tecum obscuritatem fumi et inmanitatem principis, qui in eo, sicut dicis, morabatur, lauda ibi mecum, quod uel in ipso fumo nullam partem inuenis dissimilem ceteris, ex quo in genere suo partium inter se suarum congruentiam modumque custodit. ut quadam unitate sit quod est: quae nemo sobrie considerat et non mirabiliter laudat. quid? quod etiam fumo addis uim potentiamque generandi, quando eidem quoque inhabitatores principes tribuis, ut quod hic numquam uidimus, ibi fumus fecundus sit et salubrem suis habitatoribus praebeat mansionem.
thought_title: Mani's five evil natures are full of goods
orientation: Augustine is answering Mani's description of the five natures inhabiting the land of darkness as savage and pestilential, arguing that the very things Mani lists contain goods that cannot belong to a supreme evil.
pass_a_gloss: But these five kinds, he says, inhabiting those natures were savage and pestilential. As if I had praised in them savagery and pestilence. Look, I with you blame what you accuse as evils in them; you with me praise what you yourself mention as goods in them: so you will see that you want to establish goods mixed with evils as the supreme and ultimate evil. I with you blame pestilence there; you with me praise health there; for those kinds could not have been born or nourished or inhabited that land without some health. I with you blame darkness there; you with me praise fruitfulness there; for you say the darkness is immeasurable, and yet you add 'with its own offspring,' although darkness is not bodily and this whole name is the absence of light, just as nakedness is to lack clothing and emptiness is to be void of bodily fullness; and for this reason darkness could have generated nothing, although a dark land, that is one lacking light, could have generated something. But let us pass over this for now. Yet where offspring arise, there is both a temperament suited to health and a certain numerous concord orders and builds together into unity the limbs of those being born, agreeing with one another in the peace of moderation. Who would not understand that all these things deserve greater praise than the darkness deserves blame? I with you blame there the turbid filth of the waters; you with me praise there both the very form and quality of the waters and the agreeing limbs of the swimming inhabitants, the life containing and ruling the body, and every temperament of its kind suited to health. For however much you reproach the muddy and turbid waters, yet by the fact that you call them such waters that they could both generate and contain their living things, you cannot take away from them the form of some kind of body and the likeness of parts by which they are formed and pacified into one quality, because if you take it away, there will be no body: all these things, if you are human, you perceive are to be praised. And however much you exaggerate the savagery of those inhabitants and their attacks of tearing and devastation among themselves, you still do not take away from them the numerous boundaries of forms by which the individual bodies of each of them are pacified by the equality of their limbs, and the temperament of health, and the governance of the soul reducing the parts of its body into the unity of friendship and concord: if you look at these things with human perception, you see that they are more to be praised than those things which displease are to be blamed. I with you blame there the horror of the winds; you with me praise there the breathing and nourishing nature of those same winds and the form of the body by the agreement of parts continuous and spread out: by all which things they could both generate and nourish and healthfully contain their inhabitants, and of their inhabitants, along with the other things which have been praised in all living things by the earlier reasoning, then especially the tireless and easy passages from where they wish and to where they wish, and the concordant effort of wings in flight and the not unequal motion. I with you blame there the corruption of fire; you with me praise there the generative fire and the vigorous and opportune temperament of it for those being born, both so that they might grow together and so that they might be perfected by their numbers and lineaments and so that they might be able to live and dwell there: all which things you recognize are to be wondered at and praised not only in the habitation of fire but also in the inhabitants themselves. I with you blame there the obscurity of the smoke and the monstrousness of the prince who, as you say, dwelt in it; you with me praise there that even in the smoke itself you find no part unlike the rest, from which in its kind it preserves the agreement and measure of its parts among themselves, so that by a certain unity it is what it is: which no one considers soberly and does not praise with wonder. What? That you also add to the smoke the force and power of generating, when you assign to it also its own inhabitant princes, so that what we have never seen here, there the smoke is fruitful and provides a healthful dwelling for its inhabitants.

choices.why: Renders the superlative force of 'summo' and the terminal force of 'extremo' as Mani's supposed highest evil; 'supreme evil' is the glossary term for summum malum, and 'ultimate' preserves extremo.
The adjective means 'not able to be estimated or measured'; 'immeasurable' keeps the privative force and fits the darkness Mani describes.
A technical term for the balanced mixture or condition suited to health; 'temperament' preserves the Latin root and the medical sense.
Keeps the literal adjective 'numerosa' (full of number, rhythmic) with 'concordia'; the phrase suggests a harmony ordered by number, which is Augustine's point about form.
Literal rendering of the genitive phrase; 'moderation' keeps the sense of measure and restraint, and 'peace' the concord among limbs.
The word means enormity, savagery, or monstrousness; 'monstrousness' fits the prince of smoke as a figure of horror and keeps the moral and physical excess.

pass_b_english: But these five kinds, he says, that inhabit those natures were savage and pestilential. As if I had praised savagery and pestilence in them. Look, I join you in blaming what you charge as evil in them; you join me in praising what you yourself record as good in them. Then you will see that you want to establish goods mixed with evils as the supreme and extreme evil. I join you in blaming the pestilence there; join me in praising the health there. For those kinds could not have been born, or nourished, or inhabited that land without some health. I join you in blaming the darkness there; join me in praising the fruitfulness there. For you call the darkness immeasurable, and yet you add that it has its own offspring—although darkness is not bodily, and this whole name is the absence of light, just as nakedness is the lack of clothing and emptiness is the lack of bodily fullness. For that reason darkness could produce nothing, although a dark land—that is, a land lacking light—could produce something. But let us set that aside for now. Yet where offspring come forth, there is a temperament suited to health, and a numerous concord orders and builds together into unity the limbs of those being born, each agreeing with the others in a peace of moderation. Who does not understand that all these things deserve greater praise than the darkness deserves blame? I join you in blaming the turbid filth of the waters there; join me in praising the very form and quality of the waters, and the agreeing limbs of the swimming inhabitants, the life holding and ruling the body, and every temperament of its kind suited to well-being. However much you reproach the muddy and turbid waters, by the very fact that you call them such waters that they could produce and contain their own living creatures, you cannot take away from them the form of some kind of body and the likeness of parts by which they are formed and brought into peace into one quality—because if you take that away, there will be no body at all. All these things, if you are human, you perceive are praiseworthy. And however much you exaggerate the savagery of those inhabitants and their attacks of tearing and devastation upon one another, you still do not take away from them the numerous defining limits of their forms, by which each of their bodies is brought to peace through the equality of its limbs, nor the temperament of health, nor the governing of the soul drawing the parts of its body into a unity of friendship and concord. If you look at these things with human perception, you see they are more praiseworthy than the things that displease are blameworthy. I join you in blaming the horror of the winds there; join me in praising the breathable and nourishing nature of those same winds, and the form of a body with the fitting agreement of continuous and extended parts. By all these things they could produce and nourish their inhabitants and keep them in health—and among those inhabitants, along with the other things praised in all living creatures by the reasoning above, there is especially their tireless and easy passage from where they wish to where they wish, and the concordant thrust of their wings in flight and their not-unequal motion. I join you in blaming the corruption of the fire there; join me in praising the fire that generates and thrives, and its timely temperament for those being born, so that they could grow together, and be perfected in their own numbers and lineaments, and live and dwell there. All these things you recognize are to be admired and praised not only in the dwelling place of the fire, but also in the inhabitants themselves. I join you in blaming the obscurity of the smoke and the monstrousness of the prince who, as you say, lingered in it; join me in praising that even in the smoke itself you find no part unlike the others, by which in its own kind it preserves the agreement and measure of its parts among themselves, so that what it is, it is by a certain unity. No one considers this soberly without praising it with wonder. And what of this? You even add to the smoke the force and power of generating, when you assign to it its own princely inhabitants, so that what we have never seen here, there the smoke is fruitful and offers a healthy dwelling to its inhabitants.

problems.why: lint glossary: banned rendering of summum malum; use 'supreme evil' ('ultimate evil')

fixed: The English 'ultimate evil' renders summum et extremum malum; the glossary bans 'ultimate evil' for summum malum, so I changed 'ultimate' to 'extreme' to match extremum while keeping 'supreme' for summum.
The second reported problem is the same phrase already fixed; no further edit needed.

problems.quote: the numerous boundaries of their forms
problems.why: 'Terminos' means limits/boundaries defining shape, not boundaries of forms
problems.fix: the numerous defining limits of their forms

problems.quote: No one considers this soberly and does not praise it with wonder
problems.source_quote: quae nemo sobrie considerat et non mirabiliter laudat
problems.why: Double negative: 'et non' = 'and does not'; should be 'and does not fail to praise'
problems.fix: which no one soberly considers and does not marvelously praise
problems.ruling: 'does not praise' misses double negative 'et non...laudat' = 'and fails to praise'; meaning reversed.

edits.old: the numerous boundaries of their forms
edits.new: the numerous defining limits of their forms

edits.old: No one considers this soberly and does not praise it with wonder.
edits.new: No one considers this soberly and does not fail to praise it with wonder.

fixed: Changed 'the numerous boundaries of their forms' to 'the numerous defining limits of their forms' to render 'numerosos formarum terminos' more precisely.

Changed 'No one considers this soberly and does not praise it with wonder' to 'No one considers this soberly and does not fail to praise it with wonder' to preserve the double negative of 'et non mirabiliter laudat'.

problems.quote: the form of their body with the fitting agreement of its continuous and extended parts
problems.source_quote: speciem corporis conuenientia partium continuati atque diffusi
problems.why: 'corporis' is genitive with 'speciem', 'form of a body'; English 'their body' suggests the winds' own body, but Latin is more general
problems.fix: the form of a body with the fitting agreement of continuous and extended parts

edits.old: the form of their body with the fitting agreement of its continuous and extended parts
edits.new: the form of a body with the fitting agreement of continuous and extended parts

fixed: Changed 'their body' to 'a body' because the source 'speciem corporis' has 'corporis' as a general genitive with 'speciem', not referring specifically to the winds' own body.

problems.quote: and the concordant thrust of their wings in flight and their equal motion
problems.source_quote: alarum in uolatu concordem nisum et non inparem motum
problems.why: non inparem means 'not unequal', not 'equal'; Augustine's point is asymmetry, not parity
problems.fix: and the concordant thrust of their wings in flight and their not-unequal motion
problems.ruling: non inparem means 'not unequal/uneven,' not 'equal'; Augustine stresses lack of asymmetry in wing motion, not parity between wings.

problems.why: The English marks Mani as speaker, but the following argument is Augustine's, not Mani's. 'Inquit' here introduces Augustine's imagined Manichaean interlocutor or is transitional; the whole passage is Augustine's voice.
problems.fix: But these, he says, were savage...
problems.ruling: 'inquit' marks a quoted speaker; context shows Augustine citing Mani's claim ('savage and pestilential'), not Augustine's own assertion.

problems.quote: the breathing and nourishing nature of those same winds
problems.why: 'Spirabilem' means 'breathable' (able to be breathed), not 'breathing.' The wind is breathable and nourishing to its inhabitants.
problems.fix: the breathable and nourishing nature of those same winds
problems.ruling: 'spirabilem' means 'breathable' not 'breathing'; winds are described as breathable and nourishing for inhabitants.

edits.old: and the concordant thrust of their wings in flight and their equal motion
edits.new: and the concordant thrust of their wings in flight and their not-unequal motion

edits.old: But, Mani says, those five kinds
edits.new: But these five kinds, he says,

edits.old: the breathing and nourishing nature of those same winds
edits.new: the breathable and nourishing nature of those same winds

fixed: Changed 'equal motion' to 'not-unequal motion' to match 'non inparem motum'.
Changed 'But, Mani says' to 'But these five kinds, he says' so the speaker is not marked as Mani; 'inquit' here is the imagined interlocutor or transitional, and the argument is Augustine's.

fixed.quote: No one considers this soberly and does not fail to praise it with wonder
fixed.fix: No one considers this soberly without praising it with wonder
fixed.note: The Latin 'nemo ... et non laudat' means everyone who considers this praises it, but 'No one ... does not fail to praise' says the opposite.

last_rejected.quote: you join me in praising what you yourself record as good in them
last_rejected.source_quote: lauda tu mecum, quae in illis bona ipse commemoras
last_rejected.why: lauda is imperative: Augustine commands Mani to praise, he does not report that Mani already does.
last_rejected.fix: join me in praising what you yourself record as good in them
last_rejected.ruling: English 'you join me in praising' is imperative-style parallel to 'I join you in blaming'; reads as exhortation, meaning preserved ('lauda tu mecum').

last_rejected.quote: could not have been born, or nourished, or inhabited that land
last_rejected.source_quote: uel gigni uel nutriri uel inhabitare illam terram
last_rejected.why: inhabitare is active: those kinds inhabit the land. The English makes inhabiting passive like birth and nourishment.
last_rejected.fix: could not have been born or nourished, or have inhabited that land, without some health
last_rejected.ruling: 'inhabitare illam terram' is infinitive after 'potuissent'; English 'inhabited that land' is active transitive, correctly rendered; no passive implied.

last_rejected.quote: the form of a body with the fitting agreement of continuous and extended parts
last_rejected.source_quote: speciem corporis conuenientia partium continuati atque diffusi
last_rejected.why: continuati atque diffusi agree with corporis: the body is continuous and extended, not the parts.
last_rejected.fix: the form of a continuous and extended body, and the fitting agreement of its parts
last_rejected.ruling: 'continuati atque diffusi' is genitive and could agree with partium or corporis; 'parts continuous and extended' is a defensible reading, no major meaning change.
